modules.title: Frame the conversation
modules.summary: Most difficult feedback fails before it starts. The setup determines whether the recipient hears you or defends themselves.
objectives: Distinguish a feedback conversation from a debrief, evaluation, or performance review
Choose a moment, setting, and opener that primes the recipient to listen
Pre-commit to your own outcome before opening your mouth

lessons.title: What this conversation is — and isn't
objectives: Name the type of feedback you're delivering
Decide whether this should happen at all

data.title: Feedback ≠ evaluation
data.body: A 360 review tells someone what they did. Feedback tells them what to do differently next week. Different goal, different conversation.

data.content:
Before you book the room, ask yourself: **what specific behavior do I want to change?** If you can't name it in one sentence, you're not ready to give feedback yet.

Most "difficult feedback" conversations fall apart because they bundle three things: an observation, a judgment, and a request. The recipient hears the judgment, defends against it, and never gets to the request.

data.title: Try this
data.body: Write down one sentence that finishes: *"After this conversation, I want them to ____."* That sentence is the conversation. Everything else is setup.

data.content:
**Where** matters more than people think. A coffee chat invites defensiveness. A formal one-on-one invites performance. A brief private moment after a meeting invites attention.

Three rules that tend to hold:

1. **Same day.** The longer you wait, the more the moment becomes about *you* — your hesitance, your buildup — and less about the behavior.
2. **Private but not formal.** Pull them aside; don't book a meeting room.
3. **Lead with what's at stake for them.** "I want to give you something that's going to make next week easier" beats "I have some feedback for you."
I used to schedule difficult conversations a week in advance. By the time we sat down, both of us had built so much story around it that the actual content felt anticlimactic.

modules.title: Deliver the message
modules.summary: The five-second window where the recipient decides whether to listen.
objectives: Use the SBI framing (Situation, Behavior, Impact) when stakes are high

data.content:
The first sentence sets the frame. Two opening shapes work:

- **Specific observation:** *"In yesterday's review, when the client asked about timing, I noticed you went silent for about ten seconds before answering."*
- **Concrete impact:** *"After our last sync, the engineering lead pulled me aside and said she felt cut off."*

What **doesn't** work: trait-language. *"You're being defensive."* *"You don't listen."* These are interpretations dressed as observations. The recipient hears them as character attacks and disengages.

items.title: Observation
items.desc: What you saw or heard. Time-stamped. Quotable. Anyone who was there would describe it the same way.

items.title: Interpretation
items.desc: What you decided it means. Coloured by your assumptions. Not a fact — your read.

items.title: Why mix them up?
items.desc: Because the interpretation is what bothered you. But the observation is what they can act on. Lead with the observation; reserve the interpretation for the back half.

data.content:
When the stakes are high — performance, partnership, conflict — fall back on **SBI**.

**Situation:** when and where it happened.
**Behavior:** what they did, not who they are.
**Impact:** what changed downstream — for you, the team, the client.

SBI is rigid by design. It removes the temptation to wander into trait-language.

data.title: SBI in practice
data.body: *"In the 4pm review (S), when the client asked about the Q3 numbers, you said 'we're fine' and moved on (B). Afterwards, the client emailed me asking for a follow-up — they didn't feel heard (I)."*

modules.title: Hold the response
modules.summary: How the conversation continues after the message lands. Defensive, dismissive, surprised — they all need different moves.
objectives: Distinguish a defensive response from a genuine question
Keep the conversation in 'observation' mode for at least one round
Decide when to circle back vs. close the loop

data.content:
Pushback usually takes one of three shapes:

1. **"That's not what happened."** They remember it differently. Stay in observation: *"Walk me through what you remember."* You don't have to win this round; you just need to keep the conversation grounded.
2. **"I had a reason for that."** They're explaining. Listen — sometimes you'll learn something that changes your read. If their reason holds, acknowledge it and move on. If it doesn't, return to impact: *"I hear you. The impact still landed this way."*
3. **Silence.** The hardest one. Don't fill it. Wait. Most people will continue if you give them five seconds.

modules.title: Close and document
modules.summary: The conversation ends with a specific commitment and a written follow-up. Without those, the feedback evaporates.
objectives: Get a specific, time-bound commitment before ending
Schedule the follow-up moment now, not later

data.content:
Within 24 hours of the conversation, send a 3-line written summary:

1. What we agreed.
2. When we'll check in (date / event).
3. What I'll do differently to support it.

The written summary does three things: it removes ambiguity about what was agreed, it gives them something to refer back to, and it signals that you take the conversation seriously enough to follow through.

data.title: Schedule the follow-up before you leave the room
data.body: If you don't book it now, it won't happen. Two weeks is the right horizon for behavior change to be observable.
